paragraphs.heading: Making the misses small
paragraphs.text: Least squares is a method for choosing the model that best fits a set of data. For each data point, the residual is the gap between the value actually observed and the value the model predicts. Least squares squares every residual, adds them up, and picks the model parameters that make this total as small as possible.

paragraphs.heading: Linear and nonlinear problems
paragraphs.text: Least squares problems come in two kinds, linear and nonlinear, depending on whether the model is linear in all of its unknowns. The linear kind appears in statistical regression and can be solved directly with a closed-form formula. The nonlinear kind is usually solved step by step. At each step the problem is approximated by a linear one, so the central calculation is much the same in both cases.

paragraphs.heading: A race to publish
paragraphs.text: Legendre gave the first clear and concise account of the method in 1805. He presented it as an algebraic way of fitting linear equations to data. Within ten years, it had become a standard tool of astronomy and geodesy in France, Italy and Prussia. In 1809 Carl Friedrich Gauss claimed he had possessed the method since 1795, which led to a dispute over who came first.

paragraphs.heading: Finding a lost asteroid
paragraphs.text: An early test of Gauss's approach came with Ceres. The Italian astronomer Giuseppe Piazzi discovered it on 1 January 1801 and followed it for 40 days before it vanished into the Sun's glare. Astronomers wanted to know where it would reappear without having to solve Kepler's complicated equations. Only the predictions made by the 24-year-old Gauss with least squares let Franz Xaver von Zach find Ceres again.

paragraphs.heading: Ties to probability
paragraphs.text: Gauss went further than Legendre by linking least squares to probability and to the normal distribution, which he invented along the way. In 1822 he stated that least squares gives the best linear unbiased estimate of a linear model's coefficients, when the errors have zero mean, are uncorrelated, normally distributed and equally variable. A broader form of this result is now called the Gauss–Markov theorem.
